title: Regeneration and finite stocks

blocks.heading: Regeneration and finite stocks
blocks.text: A renewable resource can replenish on a human timescale under suitable conditions. A woodland can regrow, but cutting trees faster than they regenerate can still deplete it. A non-renewable resource, such as a mineral deposit, has a finite stock that is not replaced on that timescale. Reducing waste, recovering usable materials and avoiding unnecessary extraction conserve that stock. The separating test is whether the resource itself can regenerate within the relevant human timescale, not whether people can use it repeatedly.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: An original woodland example
blocks.text: In a fictional community woodland, an estimate suggests 100 trees replace losses each year under existing conditions, but 160 are cut annually. That is a net loss of 60 trees a year if those rates persist. Because wood is renewable, controlling cutting, protecting regrowth and reducing fuel waste can help maintain it. Calling it renewable does not make the excessive extraction harmless. Regeneration depends on conditions such as surviving young trees and adequate growing conditions; a single estimate should be monitored rather than treated as a permanent guarantee.

blocks.heading: Farming is one application
blocks.text: Sustainable agriculture concerns maintaining farming and its resource base, for example by protecting soil from erosion and using water carefully. Sustainable development is broader: it also concerns services, employment and other activities. To separate the concepts, ask whether the statement specifically concerns farming practices or a wider development principle. A soil-protection example illustrates sustainability; it does not make the entire concept a farming definition.

blocks.heading: Follow the resource through use
blocks.text: Rural development in Topic 5.1 examines farming in more detail. Here, describe the resource, the way it is used and the effect on future availability. Conservation measures should fit whether the problem is loss of regeneration, waste of a finite stock or damage to the wider environment.
